claims.text: Combined sliding wear and corrosive attack induce an ultra-fine nanocrystalline or near-amorphous tribolayer in the high-entropy alloy.
The stress-induced tribolayer acts as a self-adaptive catalyst for rapid passive-film regeneration and stabilization.
Formation of this tribolayer provides a single mechanism for enhanced wear and corrosion resistance.
The proposed starting material is a homogeneous, single-phase HEA with a relatively coarse initial grain structure.
Controlled sliding in a corrosive electrolyte while varying load and corrosion potential can be used to induce and test in situ surface refinement.
Sliding-induced high strain drives dynamic microstructural refinement and creates a highly refined near-surface layer.
A softer, more deformable initial microstructure is more predisposed to dynamic surface refinement.
The high density of grain boundaries and defects in the refined tribolayer accelerates passive-oxide formation and preserves passive-film integrity.
Greater passive-film stability improves corrosion resistance.
The ultra-fine near-surface layer lowers shear strength and friction through inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer is associated with high wear resistance.
Relative to the matched baseline, the refinement-prone variant will have a lower steady-state friction coefficient in a corrosive environment.
Relative to the matched baseline, the refinement-prone variant will have a lower wear rate in a corrosive environment.
Relative to the matched baseline, the refinement-prone variant will have lower corrosion current density and greater passive-film stability.
The protective effect will be most pronounced when mechanical stress and corrosive potential are simultaneously present.
The effect will diminish at loads too low to trigger surface refinement.
The effect will diminish at loads high enough to cause excessive damage or bulk plastic failure.
The prediction may fail in an environment so aggressive that the refined passive film cannot be sustained.
A controlled comparison can combine load-dependent sliding, electrochemical measurements, and microscopy to relate tribolayer formation to friction, wear, and passive-film behavior.
Failure of the refinement-prone samples to show both more stable passivation and lower friction and wear than the baseline would falsify the proposed unifying mechanism.
